newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Danger signs lurk beneath favourable UK data.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Danger signs lurk beneath favourable UK data.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major enjoyed a remarkably good run of statistics this week after launching his election campaign, with unemployment at a six-year low and underlying inflation back under three percent.

But the headline figures which Major's Conservatives have been trumpeting as they try to narrow the opposition Labour party's double-digit opinion poll lead mask danger signals suggesting the economy could be on the verge of overheating.

Alongside the drop in February unemployment to a six-year low of 6.2 percent, announced on Wednesday, came a surge in retail sales and an unexpected jump in average earnings -- two pointers to robust consumer confidence.

Thursday's dip in underlying annual inflation to 2.9 percent in February from 3.1 percent in January masked a worrying rise in inflation in the services sector, which accounts for around 60 percent of Britain's gross domestic product.

M4, a broad measure of money supply seen as a possible warning of future inflation, surged to an annual rate of 11.3 percent in February. It has been outside the government's three to nine percent monitoring range for well over a year.
"We have passed the point in the business cycle where we can enjoy both strong growth and stable inflation," says David Mackie, an economist at J P Morgan.

"The recent pickup in average earnings growth and price inflation in the services sector cannot be ignored. They reflect growing imbalances in the economy, which will only get worse over time if growth continues unchecked."

Major and finance minister Kenneth Clarke hope to erode Labour's opinion poll lead by the May 1 election by persuading voters that their policies have produced stable growth, falling unemployment and low inflation, interest rates and taxes.
But that message does not appear to be getting through.
A Reuters/NOP poll on Tuesday showed 35 percent of voters now trust Labour more to run the economy against 26 percent for the Conservatives, even though Labour has been out of office since 1979.
Economists John O'Sullivan and Geoffrey Dicks of NatWest Markets offer two explanations for the apparent breakdown in the link between economic performance and government popularity.

Firstly, they say, the Conservatives lost their reputation for economic competence after Britain's ignominious exit from the European exchange rate mechanism in 1992 and their decision to raise taxes in breach of pre-election promises that year.
Secondly, the creation of a more flexible and open economy has increased income inequality and economic insecurity.

"A progressively smaller proportion of the electorate is experiencing the fruits of a thriving economy and income inequality is growing as the benefits of growth no longer trickle down'," the two economists said in a client note.
"Rising insecurity means that the effects of economic growth are felt to be transitory."

Not all economists are convinced that M4 is really flashing a danger signal, pointing out that it has been distorted by a surge in corporate takeover activity and the introduction of a new "repo" market in British government bonds.
"Sharp rises in the past have been followed by equally sharp falls, most notably at the start of last year," said Simon Briscoe of Nikko Europe. "We await further evidence before being convinced."
However, financial markets have responded to this week's figures by pricing in a substantial jump in official interest rates to around 6.70 percent at the end of June from six percent now.
Andrew Cates, an economist at UBS, says the jump in M4 is a cause of concern.

"It adds weight to the evidence from yesterday's labour market and retail sales data which suggested that monetary policy may be too lose at the moment and points to the strong likelihood that base rates will be raised at the first monetary meeting after the general election."
